title: Check yourself: what a stream factory hands you

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, what does `Stream.of(numbers)` produce when `numbers` is an array of primitive `int` values?

options.text: A `Stream<int[]>` holding the whole array as one element
options.says: The page says Stream.of(intArray) is a Stream<int[]> with one element; only Arrays.stream and IntStream.of turn a primitive array into a specialised stream.

options.text: An `IntStream` of the values, with no boxing on the way
options.says: The page reserves that for Arrays.stream (and IntStream.of); Stream.of does not make a primitive stream.

options.text: A `Stream<Integer>` of the values, each boxed on the way
options.says: The page says the array stays whole: Stream.of sees one element, the int[] itself.

questions.stem: Per this page, what is the best way to combine five streams?

options.text: Nest `Stream.concat()` calls, one level for each extra stream
options.says: The page warns that deeply nested concat() calls can cause a StackOverflowError.

options.text: Wrap them in `Stream.of(...)`, then `flatMap` each to its elements
options.says: The page prefers Stream.of(stream1, stream2, ...).flatMap(Function.identity()) for more than two streams.

options.text: Pass all five as arguments to a single `Stream.concat()` call
options.says: The page says Stream.concat() takes only two streams at a time.

concepts: Stream.concat joins exactly two streams, and many streams are better joined with flatMap.
Stream.of on an int array is a Stream<int[]> of one element; Arrays.stream or IntStream.of streams the values.
